name: Platform Comparison
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: No Clear Winner Among Five Approaches to the Same Problem
lesson.summary: Superconducting, trapped ion, photonic, topological, and neutral atom qubits each optimize for a different piece of the puzzle, and none dominates the others on every axis that matters.
lesson.body:
Having walked through five distinct ways of building a qubit, the obvious question is which one is actually winning. The honest answer is that there is no single winner, because the platforms are not really competing on one dimension, they are making different trades among several dimensions that all matter for building a useful computer: how many qubits you can build, how long each qubit remembers its state, how fast and accurate the gates are, how richly connected the qubits are to each other, and how much infrastructure the whole system requires.

Superconducting qubits, built by IBM, Google, and others, win on gate speed, executing operations in tens of nanoseconds, and on manufacturability, since they borrow directly from decades of semiconductor fabrication experience. They lose on coherence time, typically tens to a few hundred microseconds, and on connectivity, since each qubit is wired into a fixed, mostly nearest neighbor position on a chip that also has to survive inside an elaborate cryogenic refrigerator. Trapped ions, pursued by IonQ and Quantinuum, invert that trade almost completely: coherence times reach seconds or longer, and connectivity within an ion chain is close to universal, but gates driven by laser pulses run one to three orders of magnitude slower than superconducting gates, and long ion chains become mechanically difficult to control.

Photonic systems, built by companies like PsiQuantum and Xanadu, offer something neither of the above can: near room temperature operation and a natural fit with existing fiber optic networking, since photons are already how information travels between distant systems. Their weakness is the flip side of their strength: photons that barely interact with matter also barely interact with each other, which makes the two qubit gates a computer actually needs hard to build reliably, forcing reliance on probabilistic schemes and accepting significant photon loss along the way. Neutral atom arrays, from QuEra, Pasqal, and Atom Computing, split the difference in an interesting way: they use real atoms like trapped ions, giving them good baseline coherence, but trap them with reconfigurable laser tweezers instead of a fixed chip or a fixed ion chain, letting the array geometry itself be flexible and scale to atom counts in the hundreds to over a thousand fairly quickly, at some continued cost in two qubit gate fidelity relative to trapped ions.

Topological qubits, still the least mature of the five, are trying to change the comparison entirely by building error resistance into the physics of the qubit itself rather than trading it off against speed or connectivity, but as covered in the previous chapter, whether that physics actually delivers a controllable qubit in practice remains genuinely unresolved, so it is hard to place on the same table as the other four with any confidence.

No cross platform number, including popular single figure metrics like quantum volume, fully captures this multidimensional tradeoff, which is precisely why serious comparisons in the field specify the axis being measured rather than declaring an overall winner. A platform that looks best for one target application, say breaking a cryptographic system that needs many long, precise operations, can look mediocre for another, say a near term optimization task that tolerates more noise but needs many qubits quickly. Keeping that multidimensionality in mind is essential background for the next chapter, which asks whether any of these five approaches can actually be scaled far enough to matter.
